only where they are unset. Each worker sets its own `NEURON_RT_VISIBLE_CORES` (its core) and
`OMP_NUM_THREADS` / `MKL_NUM_THREADS` (1), whatever was exported.

## Compiled shapes

The first request at a new image size or step count compiles its graphs. The per-request
conditioning holds one modulation row per step, so the DiT graphs' input shapes depend on both.
Give the first request at each new size or step count a client timeout above its compile time.

torch-neuronx caches compiled graphs under `TORCH_NEURONX_NEFF_CACHE_DIR` (default
`/tmp/neff_cache`) and `TORCH_NEURONX_HLO_CACHE_DIR` (default `/tmp/hlo_cache`). Keep both
across containers of the same image to skip the compile. A cached graph's key covers neither the
NKI kernel sources nor the kernel library, so each cache records a digest of both (a
`KERNEL_SOURCES` file, which the first launch on an empty cache writes). A worker refuses a cache
with another digest (other kernel sources, or another neuronx-cc, which ships the kernel library),
and a filled cache with no record, and names the cache. A cache filled before the plugin recorded
digests has no record and is refused: remove it, or, if this checkout and this image built it,
record the digest with `/work/venv/bin/python -m sglang_neuron.backend.compile_cache stamp <dir>`.

## What is refused

The launcher refuses at start, naming the setting at fault:

- a launcher that has started the Neuron runtime (launch with `TORCH_DEVICE_BACKEND_AUTOLOAD=0`;
  [The runtime path](#the-runtime-path), step 1);
- CPU offload, layerwise offload, FSDP inference, torch.compile, the breakable CUDA graph, and
  SGLang's per-component placement (`--component-residency`, `--cpu-offload-components`,
  `--layerwise-offload-components`), when turned on by a flag or a `DiffGenerator.from_pretrained`
  argument (for example `--dit-cpu-offload`, `--enable-torch-compile`). SGLang's own defaults for
  them are turned off: the Neuron pipeline places and compiles its own modules;
- `--disagg-role` other than `monolithic` (disaggregated or pool serving);
- `NEURON_CC_FLAGS` or `NEURON_COMPILER_OPT_LEVEL` exported with another value than the
  profile's, and `TORCH_NEURONX_VOCAB_SHARDING_SPMD_DISABLE` exported with another value than `1`
  (torch-neuronx's vocab-sharding pass, which the plugin keeps off);
- an SGLang checkout whose functions the rank-order hook replaces or relies on differ from the
  ones at the [setup guide](../getting-started/setup-guide.md)'s commit.

The workers refuse at start, before they open their core, a compile cache whose digest differs
([Compiled shapes](#compiled-shapes)). They refuse at model load:

- CFG parallel (`--enable-cfg-parallel`, `--cfg-parallel-size` above 1): FLUX.1-dev uses
  guidance embedding;
- `--dp-size` above 1, or an `--sp-degree` other than `--num-gpus / --tp-size`;
- a `FluxPipeline` checkpoint without guidance embedding (for example FLUX.1-schnell): the
  plugin replaces SGLang's pipeline for every `FluxPipeline` checkpoint, but runs only
  guidance-distilled ones (`guidance_embeds` in `transformer/config.json`), such as FLUX.1-dev;
- `NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG` other than 2.

A request fails when:

- its height or width is not a multiple of 64, or is below 512, or its image tokens
  (`(H/16) x (W/16)`) do not split over the 64 ranks: they must be a multiple of 64, so for
  example 576 x 576 fails;
- it has a negative prompt with `true_cfg_scale > 1`.

LoRA and image-to-image are not supported.

# LingBot-World-V2 on Neuron (SGLang Diffusion)

LingBot-World-V2 (`robbyant/lingbot-world-v2-14b-causal-fast-diffusers`), a causal image-to-world model, is served in real
time over SGLang's WebSocket `/v1/realtime_video/generate` on one trn2.48xlarge, in bf16 at 480 x 832. A session starts from
an image, a prompt and a camera, and the server streams the frames chunk by chunk for as many chunks as the session asks
for. The SGLang stage is `sglang_neuron/diffusion/models/lingbot_world/lingbot_pipeline.py`; the model is `neuron_lingbot.py`
in the same directory.

## The model

A session is one SGLang request per chunk. A chunk is 3 latent frames, which decode to 12 frames (the session's first chunk
to 9).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  img["first frame"] --> enc["condition encoder (VAE)"] --> cond["chunk condition"]
  prompt["prompt"] --> umt5["UMT5"] --> tkv["text K/V (once per prompt)"]
  cam["camera"] --> prep["chunk prep: RoPE, camera modulation"]
  cond --> dit["DiT: 4 denoise passes + 1 commit pass"]
  tkv --> dit
  prep --> dit
  pool["paged K/V history"] <--> dit
  dit --> dec["streaming VAE decode"] --> frames["frames"]
```

- **DiT.** 40 blocks, TP 8 x CP 8 on NeuronCores 0-63 at LNC 1. Each chunk runs 4 denoise passes and a commit pass that
  writes the chunk's K/V into the history.
- **History.** One session's K/V lives in a paged pool on each DiT rank: an attention sink of the first latent frames and a
  recent window, one latent frame per block (`kv_pool.py`). Every pass reads it through a per-head block table with the
  paged FA2 kernel (`kernels/lingbot/fa2/`), which gathers the chunk's K/V over CP inside the kernel and, on the commit
  pass, writes the chunk into the pool in place.
- **Block.** Self-attention over the history, with the QKV projection, Q/K RMSNorm and RoPE in Wan's fused BF16 QKV kernel;
  the per-token camera modulation; cross-attention to the prompt; the FFN. The three block norms run on Wan2.2's AdaLN
  kernel. The residual stream is sequence parallel over TP: the norms run on each TP rank's rows and the TP all-reduces are
  reduce-scatters.
- **Graphs.** Eleven static graphs, compiled and warmed at load:
  - the DiT's four: the denoise pass, the commit pass, and their steady-state twins, which attend without the mask once the
    history is full;
  - two more on the DiT ranks: the text K/V of a prompt (once per prompt) and the per-chunk prep (RoPE tables and the camera
    modulation, once per chunk);
  - the role workers' five: UMT5, the condition encoder's first-chunk and continuation graphs, and the decoder's first-chunk
    and steady-state graphs (a session's first chunk has its own temporal shape).

  The DiT's launches are asynchronous: with a recorded camera the next chunk is queued whole before the current chunk's
  frames are returned.
- **Role workers.** The encoders and the decoder run apart from the DiT, so their work overlaps the DiT's next chunk: one
  16-rank world at LNC 1 on NeuronCores 64-79, started by DiT rank 0 (`roles.py`, `role_workers.py`):
  - UMT5 at TP 16 for the prompt embedding;
  - the condition encoder: the Wan VAE encoder over the first frame followed by zero frames, chunk by chunk on the
    encoder's causal cache, until that cache stops changing; later chunks reuse the last condition;
  - the streaming Wan VAE decode, chunk by chunk on its causal cache.

  Both VAE paths run on a 2 x 8 spatial grid (`distributed/autoencoders/wan_spatial_shard.py`). Payloads travel over
  queues between DiT rank 0 and the role workers; DiT rank 0 broadcasts what the other DiT ranks need.

The `LINGBOT_WORLD` env profile sets LNC 1; the role workers take NeuronCores 64-79 beside the 64 DiT ranks. The first load
compiles every graph into the NEFF cache; later loads read it.

A session is one WebSocket connection to `/v1/realtime_video/generate`. Its first message (msgpack) starts it:

```python
{
    "type": "init",
    "prompt": "...",
    "first_frame": open("image.jpg", "rb").read(),
    "size": "832x480",
    "max_chunks": 40,
    "seed": 42,
    "num_inference_steps": 4,
    "realtime_output_format": "raw",  # uint8 RGB frames; else the server encodes them
    "condition_inputs": {
        # A recorded camera: one pose per output frame ((3 * max_chunks - 1) * 4 + 1 of them).
        "camera_trajectory": {"poses": [...], "intrinsics": [...], "dtype": "float64"},
    },
}
```

The camera is either:

- a recorded trajectory (`camera_trajectory`): `poses` `[N, 4, 4]` camera-to-world and `intrinsics` `[N, 4]`
  `(fx, fy, cx, cy)` at 480 x 832, as in LingBot-World's examples (`examples/00` to `examples/05`
  in [Robbyant/lingbot-world](https://github.com/Robbyant/lingbot-world); the checkpoint does not
  carry them). The next chunk starts before the current one's
  frames are returned, and the inputs of the session's first chunks are uploaded when the session opens;
- or per-chunk `camera_actions` sent during the session, with SGLang's LingBot action semantics: a chunk without them has
  no camera condition. The next chunk cannot start before its request, so each request waits for its chunk's decode
  and returns its frames.

A new prompt sent during the session (SGLang's prompt update) conditions the session from the chunk it arrives with.

`SGLANG_NEURON_LINGBOT_TIMING_FILE` (debug) names a file the stage appends one JSON row of engine-side timings to per chunk.

  workers' 16 cores come on top.

# Kimi-K3 PD on Neuron

Kimi-K3 runs disaggregated on the plugin's [runtime](../design/runtime.md). The prefill server is one node of
Trainium3, 128 ranks at LNC1 (one rank per physical NeuronCore), eight pipeline stages of a 16-rank TP group. The
decode server is two nodes, 256 ranks at LNC1, with DSPARK speculative decoding ([PD decode](#pd-decode)). The code is
in `sglang_neuron/models/kimi_k3/` (the decode in `decode/`), and the NKI kernels it calls are in `kernels/`
(`kernels/PROVENANCE.md`).

## The model

Kimi-K3 is a hybrid MoE transformer of 93 layers: 69 KDA layers (Kimi delta attention, a recurrent linear attention)
and 24 MLA layers, and each layer's attention residuals (AttnRes) read a bank of earlier block outputs. The checkpoint's
experts are MXFP4 (`compressed-tensors`). The prefill also writes the drafter's context rows, which a decode's
speculative drafter reads.

| State | Where it lives |
|---|---|
| MLA latent rows | SGLang's hybrid linear-attention pool, with the Neuron MLA pool as its full-attention leaf: FP8 rows (`--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`), 128-token pages, stored in DCP placement over the stage's 16 ranks |
| KDA state | SGLang's request-table state pool, built as `mem_cache/state_pool.NeuronStatePool` with conv channel-major `[3 heads/tp dim, K - 1]` (the KDA kernels' layout) and upstream's temporal `[heads, dim, dim]`, both bf16 (`--mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16`) |
| Drafter rows | one row pool per drafter layer at the MLA pool's pages, on the drafter writer stage |

## The parallel layout

| Axis | Size | What it splits |
|---|---|---|
| PP | 8 | layers, `SGLANG_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=12,12,12,12,12,12,12,9` (three MLA layers a stage) |
| TP | 16 | heads, experts and the vocabulary; between layers the tokens are sequence-parallel over the 16 ranks |
| DCP | 16 | each stage's MLA rows: 128-token stripe `j` of a request lives on rank `j % 16` |

Each stage is one compiled graph a bucket (2048 and 4096 tokens). The stage boundaries move over the PP seam as three
declared kinds (`NeuronModel.pp_prefill_boundary_kinds`): the hidden rows, the attention-residual bank (one more block
a stage) and the drafter accumulator. The catalog entry sets `NEURON_SCRATCHPAD_PAGE_SIZE=512` for the stage graphs.

## Launch

The served prefill: a PD prefill with the kimi-prompt prefix cache and its host tier, paired with the
[PD decode](#pd-decode) over NIXL.

```bash
SGLANG_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=12,12,12,12,12,12,12,9 \
SGLANG_NEURON_KIMI_PROMPT_HOST_SLOTS=18000 SGLANG_NEURON_KIMI_PROMPT_HOST_STATE_SLOTS=2000 \
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path /models/Kimi-K3 --trust-remote-code --skip-tokenizer-init \
  --disaggregation-mode prefill --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl --disaggregation-bootstrap-port 8998 \
  --host <prefill address> --port 30000 \
  --pp-size 8 --tp-size 16 --dcp-size 16 --page-size 128 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --chunked-prefill-size 4096 --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 \
  --radix-cache-backend kimi-prompt --max-mamba-cache-size 512 \
  --max-total-tokens 524288 --max-running-requests 32 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
  --speculative-draft-model-path /models/<drafter checkpoint>
```

- `SGLANG_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=12,12,12,12,12,12,12,9` is the one split the stages serve: every stage ends after an MLA
  layer and has its AttnRes table. A launch without it, or with another split, is refused.
- `--skip-tokenizer-init` makes the prefill take token ids only (`/generate` with `input_ids`). For
  `/v1/chat/completions`, or `/v1/completions` with text, launch the prefill without it: the balancer sends the same
  request to both servers, and a prefill without a tokenizer fails a chat request.
- `--max-total-tokens` counts one DCP rank's rows: 524,288 tokens a rank is 8,388,608 tokens a stage.
- `--max-running-requests` bounds the requests the prefill holds, those in the stages and those whose KV is still
  going to the decode. Below `2 x --pp-size + 3` a stage idles between forwards; without the flag a pipelined PD
  prefill takes `4 x --pp-size` (32 at PP8).
- `--radix-cache-backend kimi-prompt --max-mamba-cache-size 512` is the prefix cache. The two
  `SGLANG_NEURON_KIMI_PROMPT_HOST_*` values are its host tier: 18,000 page slots and 2,000 state slots, about
  1,080 GB of host memory a node ([The kimi-prompt cache](#the-kimi-prompt-cache)).
- `--speculative-draft-model-path <drafter checkpoint>` writes the drafter's context rows, which the DSPARK decode
  reads (the decode takes the same flag); without it the prefill writes none. The prefill runs no speculative step,
  so it takes no `--speculative-algorithm`. The drafter row pools sit beside SGLang's pools on the last stage (about
  1.41 GiB a rank at 524,288 tokens). Each rank charges them against its own free memory, so a launch with the
  drafter states `--max-total-tokens`.
- The launch rules (`models/kimi_k3/launch.py`) set both roles' sampler, `SGLANG_NEURON_SAMPLER=topk_topp` (each
  request's temperature, top-k, top-p and seed on the device), and the 512 MB scratchpad page the graphs compile for;
  a launch that sets either to another value is refused.
- `--disaggregation-transfer-backend fake` in place of `nixl --disaggregation-bootstrap-port 8998` runs the prefill
  without a decode peer, for a prefill-only benchmark: no KV moves, and the PP seam still moves the stage boundaries
  over NIXL.
- The launch rules also set `SGLANG_NEURON_PP_PREFILL_EARLY_LAST_SEND=1` on the prefill when the launch does not set
  it: every stage sends a request's last chunk at its own forward ([The hand-off](#the-hand-off-to-the-decode)).

## The hand-off to the decode

The prefill's last stage samples each request's first output token with the request's own temperature, top-p, top-k and
seed (the `topk_topp` device sampler). The draw is keyed by the seed and the position of the last prompt token, so a
seeded request repeats. With a top-k, top-p or min-p filter, token 0 comes from the top 256 candidates, and the decode
filters the full vocabulary: the two differ only when the filters keep more than 256 tokens. The metadata row carries
the token to the decode, which keeps its own sampler. The settings below let the prefill send a request's last chunk and
answer the request before its release.

- `SGLANG_NEURON_PP_PREFILL_EARLY_LAST_SEND=1`: a stage other than the last sends a request's last chunk right after it
  launches that chunk's forward, with no metadata row. The last stage sends its chunk and the metadata row as soon as
  its outputs are on the host. Without it, each stage sends at its processing, after the outputs have come round the
  PP ring, and under load stage s sends about s + 1 stage times after the forward. The decode fails a room whose
  metadata row does not land in 30 s after every source reported (`sglang_patches/pd_metadata_wait`).
- `SGLANG_NEURON_PP_PREFILL_EARLY_ANSWER` (on by default): the prefill answers a request right after a stage processes
  its last chunk, if every stage sent that chunk at its forward. Without it, the prefill answers at the release, about
  pp_size + 1 chunk times later under load. SGLang's router reads the prefill's response before the decode's, and a
  chat or completions stream sends its 200 only with its first chunk, so both hold the client's first token until the
  prefill answers.
- `SGLANG_NEURON_PP_PREFILL_INFLIGHT_WAIT_PASSES` (on by default): a request whose prompt starts with the whole prompt
  of a request that waits for its release waits for that release when the release inserts more of that prompt into
  the prefix cache than the cache holds now. The next turn of a conversation then takes the hit. On the chunk-keyed tree
  this applies only to a prompt that ends on a whole chunk: the tree inserts each other whole chunk when the chunk is
  computed.
- The PD load balancer (`sglang_neuron/disaggregation/balancer.py`) streams the decode's answer as soon as the decode
  answers 200, and it watches the prefill until the decode's first event. After the stream, it keeps the prefill's
  connection open until the prefill answers, because a closed connection aborts the prefill's request.

## Serving a decode over NIXL

With `--disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl` the prefill hands each request to a decode server whose DCP size is a
multiple of 16, by whole page stripes (`disaggregation/dcp_stripes.py`, through `sglang_patches/dcp_page_transfer.py`):
MLA stripe `j` goes from prefill rank `j % 16` to decode rank `j % Cd`, the drafter rows of the decode's drafter window
go into the request's ring of rider pages, and each KDA layer's state goes as four parts (the q, k and v conv parts and
the recurrent state) to the request's decode state slot. The decode announces where these land (a page rule in its
registration), and the prefill refuses at registration a decode whose rule does not match its own pools. On hardware
the bytes the two-node DCP32 decode ([PD decode](#pd-decode)) received were bitwise equal to the prefill's.

The flags of the launch above that pair the prefill with a decode:

- `--disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl --disaggregation-bootstrap-port 8998`: the decode registers with the
  prefill's bootstrap server on that port.
- `--host <prefill address>`: SGLang binds the bootstrap server on `--host`, and the decode ranks on other nodes reach it and
  the prefill's NIXL listeners there; on loopback no decode can pair. The HTTP port is then reachable on that network
  too.
- Both servers load the patched NIXL of the [Environment](#environment) section.
- A decode can restart under a running prefill. The prefill's first libfabric WRITEs to some restarted decode ranks
  complete as canceled (EFA status 1, `Operation canceled`, prov_errno 1; ai-dynamo/nixl#2505), and later writes to
  them pass. The Kimi-K3 prefill posts such a batch's failed writes again (`sglang_patches/nixl_repost_failed_writes`,
  up to 4 rounds; each logs `NIXL re-post round`; the catalog entry's `pd_prefill_reposts_failed_writes`), so those
  requests are served. A prefill restarted under a running decode is served too.
- A decode the prefill refuses at registration (a page rule that does not match, another page size or KV dtype) is
  refused alone: the prefill logs why, fails that decode's requests with the reason on both servers, and keeps serving
  every other decode (`sglang_patches/nixl_peer_refusal`).

## PD decode

The decode server spans two Trainium3 nodes, the one decode layout the catalog entry declares
(`models/kimi_k3/decode/capability.TWO_NODE_DP8`):

| Axis | Size | What it splits |
|---|---|---|
| TP | 256 | every rank of both nodes at LNC1, as 8 DP-attention groups of attention TP 32 (four groups a node) |
| EP | 256 | the experts over all ranks |
| DCP | 32 | each attention-TP group's MLA rows |

Each step runs DSPARK with `k = 3` (4 requests a DP group, 4 verify rows each) or `k = 7` (2 requests, 8 rows) as two
programs on every rank: the verify (the 93 layers in one kernel call, the full-vocab sampler and the acceptance) and
the draft (the 5-layer MLA drafter over the request's ring of rider pages). The model's own SGLang speculative worker
(`decode/spec_worker.py`) runs them under SGLang's scheduler and overlap schedule.

Launch the decode on both nodes with the same flags and each node's `--node-rank`; node 0 serves HTTP:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path /models/Kimi-K3 --trust-remote-code \
  --nnodes 2 --node-rank <0|1> --dist-init-addr <node 0 address>:29500 \
  --tp-size 256 --dp-size 8 --enable-dp-attention --ep-size 256 --dcp-size 32 \
  --disaggregation-mode decode --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl --disaggregation-bootstrap-port 8998 \
  --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 3 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4 \
  --speculative-draft-model-path /models/<drafter checkpoint> \
  --enable-dp-lm-head --moe-a2a-backend none --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --page-size 128 --disable-radix-cache \
  --context-length 1048576 --enable-dp-attention-local-control-broadcast --scheduler-recv-interval 1 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.9 --host <this node address> --port 30000
```

- `--speculative-dspark-block-size 7 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 8` runs `k = 7`.
- The launch rules (`models/kimi_k3/launch.py`) set what the decode programs fix where the launch leaves it unset: the
  pools' tokens a rank (`--max-total-tokens`, the programs' page layout), the running requests
  (`--max-running-requests`, 32 at `k = 3` and 16 at `k = 7`) and the request slots beside them
  (`--disaggregation-decode-extra-slots`: a replica holds as many requests as its rider pool has rings). They refuse
  another value of each, a `k` the programs are not built for, a launch without the drafter or without the patched
  NIXL, and the runtime switches the programs are not built with (`NEURON_RT_A2AV_ONE_RANK_PER_CHIP`,
  `NEURON_RT_DBG_EARLY_POSTING`, `NKI_SIMULATOR`). Every rank starts its runtime with the layout's settings
  (`capability.RUNTIME_ENV`).
- Unless the launch environment sets them, the decode runs with the EFA libfabric settings (`FI_PROVIDER=efa`,
  `FI_EFA_USE_DEVICE_RDMA=1`, `FI_EFA_FORK_SAFE=1`, `FI_EFA_ENABLE_SHM_TRANSFER=0`) and `PYTHONHASHSEED=42` for its
  schedulers.
- SGLang fails a request whose KV has not arrived `SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_WAITING_TIMEOUT` seconds (300 by default)
  after the prefill took it, and that time includes the wait behind the prompts queued ahead of it. A cold 1M-token
  prompt alone takes most of the default. A workload that queues more (several long prompts at once) raises it on the
  decode. The AgentX traces at `--max-running-requests 32` on the prefill are such a workload: their first minutes
  queue the cold first turns of every session, up to 32 prompts of about 100K tokens at once, and at 300 s some of
  those requests failed with no tokens. Run them with `SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_WAITING_TIMEOUT=3600` on the decode and
  `SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_BOOTSTRAP_TIMEOUT=3600` on the prefill. The prefill fails a request whose decode has not
  sent its KV indices within the bootstrap timeout (300 s by default), and the decode then waits for KV that the
  prefill does not send; the client gets no error before the decode's timeout.
- Pair the decode (its node 0) with the prefill through the plugin's balancer:
  `python3 -m sglang_neuron.disaggregation.balancer --prefill http://<prefill address>:30000 --decode
  http://<decode node 0 address>:30000`. The prefill takes token ids only, so chat clients go through a front that
  applies the chat template; the [example](../../examples/kimi_k3/) runs the balancer and that front.
- The decode samples with each request's temperature, top-p, top-k and seed. A `/v1/chat/completions` request samples
  with the Kimi-K3 contract, as the Kimi-K3 API does: temperature 1.0 when it renders the think channel (0.6 when its
  `thinking` template kwarg is false) and top-p 0.95, whatever it sets (`SGLANG_NEURON_KIMI_K3_SAMPLING=client` keeps
  the client's values; models/kimi_k3/launch.chat_sampling_params). The contract changes the speculative acceptance:
  on real AgentX turns, which set no sampling value, top-p 1.0 in place of 0.95 gave a lower mean acceptance length
  (k = 3, temperature 1.0). A request that asks for structured
  output, min-p, `min_new_tokens`, a penalty, a logit bias, a custom logit processor, logprobs or hidden states is
  refused with HTTP 400 at the tokenizer of both servers, before the prefill computes its prompt.
- A chat request with `tools` and `tool_choice` `auto` or `none` is served. With `--tool-call-parser kimi_k3` on both
  servers, the parser reads the model's calls into `tool_calls`; without it, the calls stay in `content` in the
  model's markup. The servers apply no grammar of the tool-call parser (models/kimi_k3/launch.CHAT_TOOL_CALL_GRAMMAR),
  so a request with `tool_choice` `required` or a named tool, which needs the grammar to force the call, is refused
  with HTTP 400.
- `--disaggregation-transfer-backend fake` runs the decode alone, without a prefill: each request's KV receive
  completes at once over the pages the decode holds, for a decode-only benchmark. `SGLANG_NEURON_KIMI_K3_FORCED_AL`
  forces a mean acceptance length, for benchmarks only.
- A launch over several nodes in any other layout is refused, naming the flags it misses.

## Prefix cache

The served launch uses the kimi-prompt cache ([below](#the-kimi-prompt-cache)): a hit ends at the exact end of an
earlier prompt. The chunk-keyed tree stays available. The stage graphs keep a KDA state checkpoint at the end of every
chunk, so the chunk-keyed tree (`--radix-cache-backend neuron-chunk`) keys whole prefill chunks. A hit copies the
checkpoint at its last whole chunk into the request's state slot and restarts from there over the shared MLA pages; the
tokens after the prompt's last whole chunk (up to 4,095) are computed again. `--max-mamba-cache-size 512` gives each
stage rank 512 checkpoint slots in HBM (about 0.86 GiB a rank); a slot holds one 4,096-token chunk's state, so the slots
cover 2,097,152 tokens of chunks. The flag is required under PP: every stage's state pool must hold the same slots, or
stages evict different checkpoints.

A prompt that hits nothing takes the same time on this tree as with `--disable-radix-cache`, which runs every prompt
cold (for example a cold-prefill benchmark; drop the host-tier flags with it).

On this tree the prefill keeps at most 4 checkpoints on each cached prompt's path (`--mamba-max-states-per-path`
defaults to 4 here; SGLang's default -1 keeps one at every chunk). After each insert SGLang drops the path's shallowest
interior checkpoints and keeps the one at the prompt's end, so the state slots hold the ends of the cached prompts and a
next turn that extends a prompt hits its whole chunks. With a checkpoint at every chunk, the interior checkpoints of
long prompts fill the slots and the pool's LRU frees the leaves, the checkpoints at the prompts' ends. A value set at
launch is kept; `-1` cannot be passed (it reads as unset).

The HiCache host tier (`--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 4.7`) holds MLA pages, drafter rows and state
checkpoints on the host. At ratio 4.7 it takes 828 GiB of host memory a node: MLA pages and drafter rows of 19.7M tokens
a stage, and 2,406 checkpoint slots a rank (9.9M tokens of chunks). A hit from the host serves a 131,072-token prefix
faster than a cold prefill, and a prompt that hits nothing takes about as long as without the tier. The ranks
of a node share one budget for their host pools: the node's MemAvailable less SGLang's 10 GiB reserve, read before any
host pool is built and taken as the smallest across the nodes (the log prints it as `the 128 ranks on this host share
... GiB`). A tier that does not fit is refused, naming the bytes the node has left. On the nodes measured the budget
read 1,348 GiB, and ratio 6.25 at `--max-total-tokens 262144` starts on it without a new compile: MLA pages and drafter
rows of 26.2M tokens a stage and 3,201 checkpoint slots a rank (13.1M tokens of chunks), 1,101 GiB a node.

### The kimi-prompt cache

`--radix-cache-backend kimi-prompt` (`mem_cache/kimi_prompt_backend.py`) replaces the chunk-keyed tree and its HiCache
tier. It keeps END entries of finished prompts: an entry holds the KV pages of the tokens the prefill computed and
the KDA state of its last computed token (the entry takes the request's state slot). A next turn of a session hits the
exact end of the turn before and computes only its new tokens; on the chunk-keyed tree it computes again up to 4,095
tokens of the turn before.

- A hit shares the entry's whole pages. The request writes its new rows into the page that holds the hit's last
  tokens in place when no other request or entry uses that page past the hit (a next turn of a session). Else the page
  is copied into a page of the request first (its MLA rows, and its drafter rows on the drafter writer stage), through
  one host page with the runtime's DMA. The entry's state is copied into the request's state slot (SGLang's
  copy-on-write) before the request's first forward. The stage graphs read the prior of
  each rank from the positions its stripes hold, so a chunk can start at any token.
- Each forward that does not end its prompt also writes its end state into the request's tracking slot, and the cache
  keeps it as a chunk-end entry. A prompt that shares only those chunks with a running or finished prompt hits there.
- An entry that a next turn extends stays in the group of the new entry (keep_previous); the eviction takes the least
  recent entries first.
- The host tier (`SGLANG_NEURON_KIMI_PROMPT_HOST_SLOTS`, `SGLANG_NEURON_KIMI_PROMPT_HOST_STATE_SLOTS`) keeps the END
  entries that the device drops: their pages, their drafter rows and their KDA state. The copies to the host complete
  before the pages and the slot go back to the allocator. A host hit restores the entry and is exact too.
- The launch takes `--max-mamba-cache-size` (each entry holds one state slot) and no HiCache flags. The backend
  serves the PD prefill only.
- The host tier has separate page slots and state slots. Agentic traffic fills the state slots first: at 26,000 page
  slots and 800 state slots the state slots were full while the page slots were two-thirds empty, and the tier dropped
  the entries of sessions idle for about 15 minutes. 18,000 page slots and 2,000 state slots use the same host memory
  and keep those entries.

## What a prefill launch refuses

Another role than the PD prefill or decode; DP attention; a `--pp-size` other than 8, or a layer split other than the
served one; a TP size that does not split the KDA heads, MLA heads, experts, vocabulary or MLP widths; an EP size other
than 1 or the TP size; a DCP size other than the TP size; a chunk that is not whole stripe cycles (`128 x --dcp-size`
tokens) or is above the MX linear kernel's 8,192 rows; SGLang's default radix tree (keyed on KV pages, it would hit
inside a chunk where no state checkpoint exists); a drafter checkpoint the context rows do not implement, or a drafter
without `--max-total-tokens`; a `--speculative-algorithm`; a NIXL other than the patched overlay; a checkpoint config
without the experts' quantization, or without `rms_norm_eps`, `linear_attn_config.gate_lower_bound` or the SiTU betas;
a platform target other than Trainium3.

# GPT-OSS on Neuron

GPT-OSS runs on the plugin's [runtime](../design/runtime.md), like every other model.

The model runs the MXFP4 checkpoint (`openai/gpt-oss-120b`) on Trainium3 at LNC2 (`NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2`, two
physical NeuronCores per logical core), except the [giga-kernel decode](#the-giga-kernel-decode), which runs one rank
per physical core (LNC1). The code is in `sglang_neuron/models/gpt_oss/` and the NKI kernel calls it makes are in
`sglang_neuron/ops/`.

## The model

GPT-OSS is a mixture-of-experts transformer: every layer has GQA attention with a learned sink per head, and the even
layers attend over a sliding window. The Neuron graphs run the checkpoint's architecture on its MXFP4 expert weights as
they are. Beyond the layout changes below, two things change the numerics: the KV cache is stored in FP8, and the
prefill MoE quantizes the normed hidden states to MX FP8 for the MXFP4 expert matmuls.

- **Hidden size.** The graphs pad the hidden size to the kernels' tile and hold it in a shuffled order (the padding sits
  at the end of each quarter). The RMSNorms take their mean over the checkpoint's hidden size, so the padding changes
  nothing.
- **Experts.** The MXFP4 blocks and scales go to the kernels as they are, repacked four FP4 values to a word and tiled
  to the kernels' access pattern. The expert intermediate size is padded so that each rank's shard tiles the kernels
  (a multiple of 32 up to 512 values, of 512 above); the kernels' default of 3072 is kept wherever its per-rank shard
  tiles. The `+ 1` of GPT-OSS's SwiGLU is folded into the up-projection
  bias at load time.
- **Router.** The decode and prefill MoE kernels read the router in different hidden orders, so the model holds a copy
  for each, as it holds the post-attention norm's weight.
- **BF16 experts.** `SGLANG_NEURON_GPT_OSS_EXPERTS=bf16` runs BF16 experts dequantized from the MXFP4 blocks on the
  host, in the same padding and hidden order. The weights are the checkpoint's exact values and the activations stay
  BF16 (the MXFP4 prefill quantizes them to MX FP8), so they serve as an accuracy reference for the MXFP4 experts.
  Everything else stays the same. The decode MoE is `moe_block_tkg` on BF16 weights; the prefill norms and routes in
  torch and runs the BF16 block-sharded expert kernel with GPT-OSS's biases and clamped SwiGLU. The BF16 experts are
  about four times the MXFP4 tiles, so they are served only at `--tp-size 16 --ep-size 4`, the one layout whose shard
  fits a rank's HBM and passed the kernel check ([BF16 experts on a NeuronCore](#bf16-experts-on-a-neuroncore)).
- **FP8 KV cache.** The KV cache is FP8 (`--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`), with K in a packed layout, two tokens per
  slot, which the decode kernel reads with a DMA transpose. A page of 128 tokens holds a sliding layer's whole window,
  as the fused sliding-window prefill kernel needs. The checkpoint stores dequantization scales. The decode kernel
  quantizes by multiplying, so each scale is inverted once at load, in bf16. The prefill kernels quantize by dividing,
  so they get the inverse of that value, which is the checkpoint's scale up to bf16 rounding. The released checkpoints
  carry no KV scales, so both are 1.
  Every decode bucket reads the packed layout directly: the runtime aligns the sliding layers' trimmed table to
  2 x LNC x 128 tokens, and the launch refuses a `--context-length` at which a full layer's bucket could not (rounded
  up to 256 tokens, it must be a multiple of 512).

## The graphs

A prefill server builds the prefill graph, a decode server the decode graph, and an aggregated server both, sharing one
copy of the weights on the device.

The prefill runs one request per forward, padded to its bucket. Between the layers the tokens are sequence-parallel
over attention TP. One prefill layer:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  n["input norm, fused with the previous layer's residual add"] --> qkv["QKV, RoPE and K/V write: one kernel"]
  qkv --> att["attention over the cached prefix and the bucket, in segments"]
  n --> swa["a qualifying sliding-window layer: one fused kernel instead"]
  att --> m1["residual add, norm, MX FP8 quantize and route: one kernel"]
  swa --> m1
  m1 --> g["rows gathered to the expert ranks, in per-expert blocks"]
  g --> ex["block-sharded MXFP4 expert kernel"]
  ex --> red["reduced back to each rank's tokens"]
```

A sliding-window layer qualifies for the fused kernel when its rank holds at least two KV heads, on the FP8 cache, with
a page that holds the whole window. The routing is packed into each token's row. Only the sampled rows reach the LM
head.

The decode runs two kernels per layer:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  ab["attention block: input norm, QKV, RoPE, attention with sinks over the paged cache, K/V write, output projection"]
  ab --> mb["MoE block: post-attention norm, router, experts"]
```

The attention masks are built once per step, one for the sliding-window layers and one for the full layers, and the
sliding layers read a block table trimmed to the pages their window can reach.

The prefill graph and the per-layer decode graph end in the device sampler. The LM head's vocabulary shards stay on
their ranks and the sampler reduces over them, so the logits never leave the device. The giga-kernel decode picks its
tokens in its own fused tail instead.

## Parallel layouts

How each layout maps onto ranks, groups and collectives is in [Parallelism](../design/parallelism.md#gpt-oss) and
[GPT-OSS's experts](../design/parallelism.md#gpt-osss-experts).

**Prefill** runs attention tensor-parallel. The kernels bound one rank's share of the attention, so the prefill needs
an attention TP of at least four. The experts are split over `--ep-size` ranks, and each expert's intermediate
dimension over the remaining TP ranks of its row.

**Decode** on a decode server runs DP attention (`--enable-dp-attention --dp-size N`): each replica attends over its
own requests with an attention TP of at least eight, so that every rank holds one KV head, which is what the decode
kernel takes. On an aggregated server, which refuses DP attention, the decode graph runs attention TP over all
`--tp-size` ranks, again at least eight. Under DP attention the experts span the replicas through EP, and the
exchange around them depends on the step's token count over the fleet:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  t["each replica's tokens"] -->|"otherwise"| ga["gather every replica's tokens"]
  ga --> e1["experts"] --> r1["reduce; each replica keeps its own"]
  t -->|"128 or more, splitting evenly over the world"| ag["all-gather over the world"]
  ag --> e2["experts"] --> r2["reduce-scatter over the world: a token shard per rank"]
```

On the second path the attention output is reduce-scattered over attention TP to match, and the layer ends with an
all-gather over attention TP.

The compiled shapes come from the server arguments. The prefill compiles one graph, of the chunk
(`--chunked-prefill-size`), which must be one of the segmented kernel's KV segment tiles (512, 1024, 2048, 4096 or 8192)
and a multiple of the attention TP size; `--cuda-graph-bs-prefill` below the chunk is refused. The decode compiles one
graph per batch size, each over the whole context. The DP-attention decode runs one size, `--max-running-requests`
divided over the DP replicas, and refuses a `--cuda-graph-bs-decode` size below it. An aggregated server compiles
`--max-running-requests` and each power of two below it, or instead of the powers of two the smaller sizes
`--cuda-graph-bs-decode` lists. The context is `--context-length`, rounded up to 256 tokens; the multiple-of-512 rule is
under FP8 KV cache above. `--max-total-tokens` sizes the KV pool, whose page count is a dimension of the compiled
graphs.

## The giga-kernel decode

A decode server laid out as `--tp-size 128 --dp-size 16 --enable-dp-attention --ep-size 128` runs the giga-kernel
decode: every decoder layer of a step in one call of nkilib's giga kernel, and the final norm, LM head and greedy pick
in one more. The layout is what selects it (`serving_policy.giga_decode_layout`). Its 128 ranks are the node's 128
physical NeuronCores, one rank per core, so the platform runs this server at one logical core per physical core
(`NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=1`, set for the launch; every other server keeps 2). Each of the 16 DP groups has
eight attention ranks, and every rank holds one whole expert. The prefill side doesn't change: TP4 prefill replicas feed
it as they feed the per-layer decode.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  ids["the step's token ids"] --> prep["vocabulary-shard ids and attention control"]
  prep --> gk["giga kernel: every layer's TP attention, KV write and EP MoE"]
  gk --> ag["all-gather of every rank's rows"]
  ag --> tail["fused tail: final norm, LM-head slice, logits exchange, greedy pick"]
  tail --> own["this DP group's tokens"]
```

The code is in `sglang_neuron/models/gpt_oss/giga/`, with the two kernel wrappers in
`sglang_neuron/ops/gpt_oss_giga_decode.py` and `sglang_neuron/ops/gpt_oss_giga_tail.py`:

- At load, each kernel argument's per-layer weights are stacked into one `[L, ...]` tensor, in the kernel's layouts: the
  gate/up MX scales in the PACK64 order the kernel reads, the V scale folded into the output projection, and the router
  in float16.
- The KV pool allocates each pair of layers (a sliding-window layer and the full layer after it) as the two halves of
  one K tensor and one V tensor, the form the kernel takes. Each layer's cache is still a view of its own half, so the
  disaggregated transfer moves the same per-layer pages it moves for the per-layer decode.
- The LM head is sharded over all 128 ranks. The fused tail exchanges the logits in two all-to-all hops, first within
  a device and then across the devices, and every rank ends with its DP group's greedy tokens.
- Each step's inputs are built in one numpy pass with a single upload (`giga/runtime.py`). The 128 ranks share their
  node's CPUs and every step waits for the last rank's launch, so the host work per step stays as small as it can be.
- The graph compiles with a DMA-order schedule for the kernel (`giga/dma_order.json`); without it the kernel would
  still run correctly, only slower. The compiler arguments name the schedule by its content, so the compile cache
  can't serve a decode compiled with another schedule. After the decode warms up, the server checks that the
  schedule fits the compiled graph (at least 80% of its constraints name the kernel call's instructions) and refuses
  to start if it doesn't. `tools/giga_schedule.py` rewrites the schedule for a graph whose kernel call has moved.

On this decode server the platform sets nkilib's QK-swapped attention path (`NKILIB_EXPERIMENTAL_ATTN_TKG_NO_SWAP=0`),
the path the giga kernel is validated on, and the kernel-build flags the schedule was derived on (`models/catalog.py`).
It refuses:

- a sampler other than greedy (`SGLANG_NEURON_SAMPLER`), top logprobs (`SGLANG_NEURON_MAX_TOP_LOGPROBS` above 0), and
  requests that ask for logprobs (`return_logprob`), since the fused tail returns tokens only;
- the model at 128 ranks in any other layout, and a launch `NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG` that contradicts the layout;
- any other flag of the giga kernel's build in the launch environment (every variable nkilib reads under
  `GIGA_KERNEL_FLAG_PREFIX`, `models/catalog.py`, beyond the seven the platform pins): the kernel reads every one, some
  change its numerics, and several read any value, `0` too, as on;
- a `SGLANG_NEURON_MAX_INFLIGHT_LAUNCHES` outside 2 to 4, the launched steps its result processing trails by;
- a `--max-running-requests` whose per-group batch isn't a multiple of the DP group's eight attention ranks (the
  kernel splits each DP group's rows over them; a multiple of 128 always works);
- layers that don't alternate sliding and full attention in pairs, or more than the kernel's 18 pairs; other than one
  whole expert per rank; different KV scales per layer;
- an image whose kernel library has no fused tail, no sorted hardware top-k, or a giga kernel that reads its gate/up
  scales unpacked, and a neuronx-cc older than 2.28.4568.0, the build the tail's sorted top-k is validated with (the
  setup guide's).

## The SGLang patches

Two upstream checks would refuse GPT-OSS on Neuron. Both patches are installed in every process, the launching one
included, because SGLang consults them while it resolves the server arguments. Both are inert for any other model.

- `sglang_neuron/sglang_patches/gpt_oss_backend_check.py`: SGLang asserts that a GPT-OSS server's attention backends are
  on a fixed list of its own backends. For a GPT-OSS launch on the Neuron backend, the check runs with a listed backend
  for that one call. The server arguments are not modified.
- `sglang_neuron/sglang_patches/quantization_registry.py`: SGLang registers its MXFP4 config on other platforms only,
  and refuses a quantization name its registry lacks before it asks the platform. The patch adds an inert config under
  `mxfp4`, which the platform returns too; every other model's host refuses a quantized checkpoint.

Each patch checks the source of the function it relies on against the SGLang it was written for, and refuses to install
on another.

GPT-OSS itself is registered through SGLang's out-of-tree model package. For a GPT-OSS launch the platform sets
`SGLANG_EXTERNAL_MODEL_PACKAGE=sglang_neuron.models.gpt_oss` and `NKILIB_EXPERIMENTAL_ATTN_TKG_NO_SWAP=1` (`0` on the
giga-kernel decode) for every process it starts (declared in `sglang_neuron/models/catalog.py` and set by
`apply_model_settings` in `sglang_neuron/platform.py`), which also keeps SGLang from importing its in-tree models there.
Leave both unset.

## Serving

The platform sets `TORCH_NEURONX_ENABLE_STREAMS=1` and `NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2` (`1` on the giga-kernel decode) for
the launch; leave them unset.

The commands below run inside the container, with the checkpoint mounted at `/models`; the
[container guide](../guides/container.md) has the `docker run` for one node and for prefill/decode over two. The
[example](../../examples/gpt_oss_120b/) has both prefill/decode layouts as scripts, the giga-kernel decode as a second
decode command, and [examples/README.md](../../examples/README.md#run-a-model) gives the order to run them.

The decode compiles at `-O2` and the prefill at the default `-O1`. A decode that traces the device sampler's exact

```bash
  --max-running-requests 64 --max-total-tokens 655360 --mem-fraction-static 0.8 \
```

```mermaid

  client["client"] --> bal["balancer"]
  bal --> P["prefill server: five replicas, attention TP4, EP2"]
  bal --> D["decode server: eight DP-attention replicas, attention TP8, EP64"]
  P -->|"KV over NIXL"| D
```

The local control broadcast sends control requests to every DP leader directly, so every rank of the decode sees them

inference](../design/disaggregated-inference.md#configuration).

```bash

```

```bash
  --tp-size 128 --dp-size 16 --enable-dp-attention --ep-size 128 --enable-dp-attention-local-control-broadcast \

  --tokenizer-worker-num 4 --detokenizer-worker-num 4 --host <decode node> --port 30000
```

At the giga kernel's step one detokenizer streaming every token falls behind 128 streams, so this decode streams every
fourth token (the first and the last at once) and runs four detokenizer processes.

### Chat completions and tool calls

GPT-OSS answers in the harmony format: its reasoning on the `analysis` channel, then the answer on the `final` channel.
The launches above pass no parser, so a
`/v1/chat/completions` answer's `content` holds the channel markup as well, for example
`<|channel|>analysis<|message|>... 17*20=340, 17*3=51, sum=391. So answer 391.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>391`. To
serve chat clients, add SGLang's GPT-OSS parsers to the aggregated server, or to both servers of a disaggregated
deployment:

```bash
  --reasoning-parser gpt-oss --tool-call-parser gpt-oss
```

With them, `content` holds only the answer (`391`) and `reasoning_content` the reasoning, in streamed answers too, and a
request that offers `tools` gets `tool_calls` back with the finish reason `tool_calls`. The parsers run in SGLang's
tokenizer and detokenizer processes and cost no decode time: on the giga-kernel deployment above, SGLang's serving
benchmark (8,192 tokens in, 1,024 out, 128 requests in flight) measured the same median TPOT with and without them
on the same two nodes.

## BF16 experts on a NeuronCore

The BF16 experts' two kernel calls were compared with their torch paths on one NeuronCore (trn3, LNC2), at each
layout's per-rank expert shard, with the checkpoint's experts of layers 0, 18 and 35 (whose down projections differ a
hundredfold in scale), on both EP ranks of an EP-TP row: `moe_experts_blockwise_swiglu` at prefill calls of 1024, 4096
and 8192 tokens (routed by the graphs' top-k), and `moe_block_tkg` without scales at decode batches of 1 to 128. A case
passes with no NaN or Inf, `max |kernel - torch| <= 1e-5 + rtol * max |torch|` (nkilib's own bound: rtol 2e-2 for
`moe_cte`, 1.1e-2 for `moe_block_tkg`), every row's cosine at least 0.999, and the unserved rows and padding columns
within the same bound.

| Layout | Expert shard a rank | Prefill cases | Decode cases | BF16 experts a rank | Served |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TP16 EP4 | intermediate 1024, 32 experts | 18 of 18; worst row 0.66%, cosine 0.99998 | 48 of 48; worst row 1.82%, cosine 0.99994 | 21.7 GB | yes |
| TP8 EP2 | intermediate 1024, 64 experts | 18 of 18; worst row 0.73%, cosine 0.99997 | 45 of 48: three batches of 4 and 8 are 2 to 3 bf16 ulps over the max-abs bound (1.25 times it at worst), their rows within 0.7% | 43.5 GB, over a logical core's 38.6 GB | no |
| TP16 EP16 | intermediate 3072, 8 experts | 7 of 18: NaN rows at 4096 and 8192 tokens | 45 of 48: three over the max-abs bound (1.39 times it at worst) | 16.3 GB | no |

TP16 EP4 runs the attention at TP16 (four query heads a rank), where the MXFP4 deployments run TP8. Any other
layout is refused at launch, naming the expert shard it would give the kernels.

## What is refused

A launch the graphs can't serve fails at startup, naming the setting at fault:

- a checkpoint that is not MXFP4, or whose dtype is not bfloat16;
- a KV cache other than `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, or a page size other than 128 (a launch without `--page-size`
  gets 128);
- a target other than Trainium3;
- `SGLANG_NEURON_GPT_OSS_EXPERTS` at a value other than `mxfp4` or `bf16`; and `bf16` on the giga-kernel decode (which
  runs the MXFP4 experts in its one kernel), at any layout but `--tp-size 16 --ep-size 4` (the refusal names the
  layout's expert shard, or what its measurement found), with DP attention, or with a `--chunked-prefill-size` over 8192
  or a `--max-running-requests` over 128, past the call sizes its kernels were measured at;
- `NKILIB_EXPERIMENTAL_ATTN_TKG_NO_SWAP` at a value other than the platform's: `1`, since the per-layer decode
  attention is validated on nkilib's non-swapped QK path, and `0` on the giga-kernel decode, whose attention is
  validated on the swapped one;
- a prefill attention TP under four, and a decode attention TP under eight;
- DP attention without `--ep-size`; attention heads that do not split evenly over the attention TP ranks; KV heads that
  neither split over those ranks nor replicate evenly across them; and experts that do not split over the EP size;
- a checkpoint whose `layer_types` do not slide the even layers and attend fully on the odd ones;
- a `--context-length` that, rounded up to 256 tokens, is not a multiple of 512;
- an expert intermediate shard the prefill expert kernel cannot take (use more EP and fewer TP ranks per expert): this
  one at the prefill graph's warm-up compile, after the weights have loaded;
- `SGLANG_EXTERNAL_MODEL_PACKAGE` set to another package, or an SGLang whose patched functions changed;
- `--enable-dp-attention` on an aggregated server, whose DP ranks would run prefill and decode graphs in the same step:
  serve DP attention disaggregated;
- a DP-attention decode without `--enable-dp-attention-local-control-broadcast` or `--max-running-requests`, or with
  `--scheduler-recv-interval` other than 1, `--sleep-on-idle`, `--disable-overlap-schedule`, two-batch overlap, or a
  decode batch size below the per-DP batch in `--cuda-graph-bs-decode` or `--cuda-graph-config`
  ([Disaggregated inference](../design/disaggregated-inference.md#configuration));
- on a role that prefills, a `--cuda-graph-bs-prefill` count below the chunk, since GPT-OSS compiles the chunk's graph
  alone, and a chunk (`--chunked-prefill-size`, divided by the DP size under DP attention) that is not one of the
  segmented kernel's KV segment tiles, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096 or 8192: these two when the runtime builds its graphs,
  after the weights have loaded;
- a launch `NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG` that contradicts the layout's degree, 2, or 1 on the giga-kernel decode. A value
  equal to the host's default is replaced and logged instead, since torch-neuronx's import writes that default into
  an unset variable and the launch's own value cannot be told from none;
- the features every model refuses ([What a launch refuses](../design/runtime.md#what-a-launch-refuses)).

An in-place weight update is refused when it is requested.

# GLM-5.2 decode giga kernel

One NKI kernel runs a decode step's 78 layers on every rank: DSA sparse MLA attention with its indexer, the MXFP4
all-expert MoE, the LM-head tail and its sampler. The `decode/mtp/` fork is the MTP draft layer's
rows-layout chain, with attention, indexer, MLP and MoE sub-kernels of its own.

Every served decode point (`models/glm52/points.py`: `128k`, `1m`) runs this copy;
`models/glm52/decode/kernel_limits.py` (`DECODE_KERNEL_PACKAGE`) pins it. `models/glm52/ops/gk_decode.py` wraps the giga kernel
and `ops/mtp_draft.py` the draft chain.

## What the host reads from the copy

- Its limits, from the giga kernel's and the draft chain's source without importing them
  (`models/glm52/decode/kernel_limits.py`): the indexer keys a rank serves, the latent stacks, and the options it takes.
  `check_kernel_copy` refuses a geometry above them before any trace.
- The 640-byte static KV row (`decode/attention/mla/kv_row_layout.py`): bf16 `k_pe` divided by
  the static scale, then the e4m3fn latent in the kernel's channel order. It is the only row the copy reads, and the
  prefill writes it directly, so a page moves from the prefill to the decode without translation.
- The MXFP4 weight conversion (`decode/mxfp4_checkpoint.py`), which the weight store uses.

## Knobs

The copy reads `GLM52K_*` and `GLM52_*` knobs when it is imported or traced, each with its own default (most off). A
served point's values are its launch settings (`models/catalog.py` from `points.py`); `kernels/compile_knobs.py` puts
each set knob into the kernel digest that keys the NKI compile cache, so a knob change recompiles.

## The indexer's top-k

A rank's indexer keys are dealt over the CP group in `idx_block_size`-key blocks. The local stage selects the
rank's top `index_topk`; a shard above 32,768 keys is ranked in a power of two of equal chunks, then the chunk
winners. The packed CP merge selects the global top-k in NKI (`../topk_select.py`), each winner carrying its shard-local
key as the payload; a chunked shard takes the wide rounds, each rank keeping its share of the global top-k. At the
1M point the chunk-dealt pool spreads a sequence's chunks over the pool members (`models/glm52/layout/decode/idx_pool.py`).

## Provenance

`../PROVENANCE.md` lists where the copy comes from and every edit to it; `MANIFEST.json` records every file's sha256.

"""In-graph torch glue of one Kimi-K3 DSpark decode step: carry, windows, embedding, acceptance, drafter inputs.

These functions are traced into the verify and draft device programs, so each keeps its torch ops, dtypes, shapes and
op order: they decide the HLO around the kernels. Every rank value and collective comes in as an argument.

Row order: the host keeps the Q = 1 + k rows of a request together (request-major, row ``b * Q + j``); the kernels
take token-major rows (row ``j * B + b``) (``to_token_major``, ``to_request_major``).

Async steps: the host's row 0 ``N`` of a carried request runs ahead of the true row 0 by the drafts that the last step
rejected (0 to k), so the host gives each request a window of candidate positions from ``N - k`` and the graph takes
its rows at the true row 0 (``carry_spec_state``, ``window_rows``). A fresh row takes its replay length and state
position from the host; any other row takes them from the outputs of the last step.

Probabilistic drafts (``accept_probabilistic_drafts``): the drafter draws each draft of a sampled request from its
distribution q over at most 256 candidates S of the row; the verify takes one joint accept length from the cumulative
ratio ``c_i = min(1, c_{i-1} p(d_i) / q(d_i))`` (``block``) or tests each draft (``standard``), and draws the stop row
from ``max(c p - q, 0)`` as a mixture of its part on S and the target outside S. The shapes are static.
"""

from typing import Callable, NamedTuple

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch import Tensor

"""Row flag: every logit of the row is -inf (no token is allowed)."""

"""Row flag: a greedy kernel token is the last id, the clamp target of a NaN row."""

"""A temperature below this samples greedily."""

"""Tokens of one MLA kernel page, which is also the CP interleave."""

"""The draft slots of the MLA drafter kernel: ``u_draft`` is ``[B, 7]`` whatever k is."""

"""The q-list width of the drafter: the top ``256 / tp`` candidates of each of the ``tp`` vocab shards."""
